# 12-transload: sources

Back-test entry `12-transload.yaml`. Transload, YC Spring 2026 (Launch YC 2026-05-18; Launch HN 2026-06-09). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **HN**: Launch HN thread, founder post and replies. https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48463273 (read whole through the HN Algolia API, https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48463273)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QP2-transload-we-measure-freight-with-security-cameras
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/transload
- **TTN**: Transport Topics, "Precision Pricing" (carriers' dimensioners in terminals). https://www.ttnews.com/articles/precision-pricing
- **FW**: FreightWaves, "Gov't lawsuit against YRC shines light on LTL reweighing practices". https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices
- **DTS**: Diversified Transportation Services, "How does a dimensioner work in a real-life environment". https://www.dtsone.com/dimensioner-actually-work-real-life-environment-2
- **SMC**: SMC³ blog, "Where LTL dock operations can improve shipper/carrier relations". https://smc3blog.com/where-ltl-dock-operations-can-improve-shipper-carrier-relations/

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the practitioner role, `dock_supervisor`; context actor).**
- HN: "transload helps LTL trucking companies measure freight dimensions using the security cameras already installed in their terminals." and "In practice, many terminals only measure a sample of their shipments."
- TTN (Estes): "A dockworker uses a forklift to drive the freight up to the landing zone".
- *My choice:* no public source names a job title (the shortlist scores this item 2 for that reason). I chose the **dock supervisor**, the person who runs a shift on the cross-dock and decides which freight goes to the dimensioner. That is where "only measure a sample" happens. A dock worker scans but does not decide what gets measured, and the revenue team only sees the result later.

**2. What (the job).**
- HN: "If a shipment is larger than the shipper reported, the carrier undercharges for it while still giving up the same amount of trailer space."
- HN: "carriers lose money every day because shippers understate dimensions and LTL is priced by volume."
- Job wording ("get every shipment billed at its true size without slowing the dock") is mine, combining these quotes with item 3's congestion point.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- HN: "The obvious fix is to measure every shipment, but thats impossible in a busy freight terminal. Dedicated dimensioning systems work for freight that passes through them, but they add forklift travel, create dock congestion, and change the normal flow of work."
- TTN: "We dimension a little more than 35% of our freight" (Estes). YRC about 40%, Oak Harbor about 8%.
- *My choice:* occasion "dock shift"; recall window 5 working days; Frequency 4 to 5 working days out of 5. The source says it happens on every busy shift but gives no count.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- HN reply: "Our wedge is underbilling in LTL trucking with ~10k relevant cross-docking warehouses across the US and Europe."
- YC-L: over 2 million irregular items move across the US by truck every day (as read on the page).
- *My choice:* market US. The company is based in Munich, but the US is the market its posts name first. Segment: dock supervisors at LTL carriers' cross-dock terminals in the US.

**5. Who pays (decision-maker role, buyer and payer, purchase friction).**
- HN: "We are currently working with several LTL carriers." YC-C: "transload helps logistics companies measure shipments using the security cameras they already have." YC-L asks: "Do you know any trucking company or warehouse owners?"
- *My choice:* the carrier pays. The **terminal manager** chooses (role id `manager`), and head office has to agree. Public material does not say who signs.
- Purchase friction, tested "An IT review of camera access": my choice. HN (kotaKat) gives a nearby signal: "you may need to look into NTEP approval before this is being used for legal trade... dimensioning is a big deal." Shared camera footage is the step most likely to need sign-off.

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- HN: "Our system has two main steps: connect a barcode scan to the right object in the video, then estimate that object's dimensions in real-world units."
- HN: "Dock workers already scan freight as part of the normal workflow. Each scan gives us a timestamp and a handling-unit ID."
- HN: "identify under-dimensioned shipments, attach visual evidence, and help carriers correct the billing or classification."
- HN: "Nearly every warehouse already has CCTV." Compatibility tests whether the cameras cover the doors where freight is scanned. That condition is my choice, because the mechanism needs it.
- Adoption friction, "Review each shipment the system flags": my choice. The output is a flag with evidence, and someone on the dock or in billing has to act on it.

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- HN reply: "We're seeing ~$50k/site/month in recoverable revenue from fixing that alone."
- YC-C: the founders put catching these differences at about $50k per site per month in rebillings and improved trailer utilization (as read on the page).
- *My choice, derived from the value claim:* no price is public. The founder's price belief is **$4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal**, about a tenth of the $50k claim, the share a value-priced B2B tool commonly takes. The cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$30,000 to $50,000 a month**. The top is the founders' $50k. The low end allows for the HN post's "roughly 10%" mis-measured against YC-C's "15%" (10/15 of $50k, rounded down). Ability to pay is derived by code: 8% to 20%, small share.
- `hourly_rate` $30: my choice, a round figure for an LTL dock supervisor's loaded hour. No source gives one.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- HN: "After spending time with customers and talking to more than 50 trucking companies, we realized that forklift routing was not the pain people kept bringing up. Freight dimensions were."
- HN: "For one customer, roughly 10% of checked shipments had dimension errors."
- HN: "Jago grew up close to this industry through his family's LTL trucking and cross-docking business."
- YC-C: "For our customers, 15% of shipments turn out to be bigger than what the sender claimed."

## The respondents

No public first-person account by an LTL dock supervisor or terminal manager was found. HN has no commenter who works on a dock, and searches of trucking forums and Reddit returned nothing on dimensioning. The shortlist warns not to invent customer voices. So **every story below is the author's invention, filling that gap**. Each is built on the trade-press facts named after it, and no real person's name is used.

Dock supervisors (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Marcus Bell: author's invention, filling a gap: no dock account public. Built on HN ("many terminals only measure a sample") and TTN (dimensioner lanes, Estes' 35%).
- Rosa Delgado: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on HN ("add forklift travel") and TTN (a disputed pallet a dimensioner photo showed was "72 inches tall").
- Dwayne Okafor: author's invention, filling a gap: the sceptic whose terminal already dimensions a large share. Built on TTN (Estes "a little more than 35%", YRC about 40%, "there are no long waiting lines").
- Teresa Lindqvist: author's invention, filling a gap: a small terminal with no dimensioner. Built on HN (sample only) and DTS ("Carriers base the size on the longest measurements in each direction").
- Hamid Rahimi: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Kenji Watanabe: author's invention, filling a gap. Built on FW: the dock staff "in charge of reweighing the freight" were separate from the "weigh and research department". So he picks the escape "Someone else does the checking".
- Lakisha Freeman: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). The sensitivity is grounded in FW's account of a federal lawsuit over reweighing practices.
- Brian Kowalczyk: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (no shift with unmeasured freight in the window).
- Priya Nair: author's invention, filling a gap: a terminal with a dimensioner on every inbound door, one down for an hour. Built on TTN (Estes "multiple units at our facilities").
- Samuel Mensah: author's invention, filling a gap: peak volume blocks the lane. Built on HN ("create dock congestion") and TTN (YRC: "we don't want a dockworker sitting and waiting on a dimension machine").
- Graciela Ortiz: author's invention, filling a gap: nothing measured, found at the trailer. Built on HN ("still giving up the same amount of trailer space") and SMC ("you're seeing more and more reclassifications on carriers' docks").
- Jerome Whitfield: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

Terminal managers (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only, no story by rule):
- Alan Brooks: author's invention, filling a gap: a manager whose own audit roughly matches HN's "~$50k/site/month".
- Fatima Benali: author's invention, filling a gap: counts the cost as inspection staff hours, not lost revenue (FW: a weigh and research department of "between 80 to 90 people" at one carrier).
- Ray Castellano: author's invention, filling a gap: cannot put a number on it, and head office decides.
- Nadine Fournier: author's invention, filling a gap: a smaller terminal with a smaller loss.
- Oluwaseun Adebayo: author's invention, filling a gap: a large hub where the loss is above the founders' figure.
- Greg Halvorsen: author's invention, filling a gap: the manager whose dimensioners already catch it and who sees no cost (TTN: Estes "using 129 dimensioners", "payback timeline is three to six months").
- Mei Lin Chou: author's invention, filling a gap: a mid-size loss and a long IT review.
- Dale Pruitt: author's invention, filling a gap: counts re-measuring hours, and someone else had to agree.

## Open

- **No job titles in the public material.** The dock supervisor and the terminal manager are my choices (item 1, item 5). A back-test may find the founders would have named the carrier's revenue or pricing team as the payer instead.
- **Price is derived, not stated.** $4,000 to $6,000 a month and the $30,000 to $50,000 cost are my derivations from the $50k value claim. Treat the commercial vector's reading as a reading of my derivation as much as of the founders' belief.
- **All twenty respondents are invented.** No dock or terminal manager voice was found in public. The stories are grounded in trade press (TTN, FW, DTS, SMC) and in the founders' HN post.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The founders' benefit is labelled "Every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample" under the nearest code, `easier_recovery` (revenue recovery). The label carries the meaning; the code name is approximate.
- **Decision-maker role id is `manager`.** The checker builds the Buyer and payer sentence from the role id ("The manager decides, and head office has to agree."), so the id was shortened from `terminal_manager`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional for a back-test. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM HOLDING_UP, SOLUTION PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Compatibility: camera access needs help or is missing at 3 of 7), COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice: most managers see far less than $30,000 to $50,000 a month).

whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line, since both are real answers from people on a dock, so nothing needed keeping out.

founder.order_why: It goes from market to context, problem, solution and then sending, which is how I'd explain Transload myself: define the dock shift, show the unmeasured freight, then show the camera fix.

founder.missing: The commercial side: nothing asks who pays or decides, which for me is the terminal manager with head office agreeing, rather than the dock supervisor being interviewed. Nothing asks my price ($4,000 to $6,000 a month per terminal), what the undercharging costs a terminal ($30,000 to $50,000 a month), or about purchase friction such as an IT review of camera access. screens.why1: I have just listed what they must do to start, and Solution 4 of 4 needs the one effort worth testing, so it is obvious why Keel asks me to pick here.
screens.why2: The question and both efforts are plain to me on first read, and 'flags' is the word I use for what the system produces.
screens.why3: After talking to more than 50 trucking companies, I know the two sticking points are camera access and someone having to act on each flag, so I can answer this from what I have seen.
screens.why4: The two efforts are distinct and mine, but camera access is usually a manager or IT call rather than a dock supervisor's, so that option sits oddly against the person being tested.
screens.why5: My picked effort appears word for word in the belief and the test, and the belief still means what I typed.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop a dock supervisor? Options: Review each shipment the system flags / Get the terminal's OK to use the dock cameras for measuring

screens.why1: Right after setting out the solution and just before the study goes out, it makes sense to decide whether to ask respondents to try it, since I'm hunting for carriers to work with.
screens.why2: Offer a pilot and the hint are plain to me, but the hint leaves me a second read on who 'people' are and whether 'try this for real' means a dock supervisor or a carrier that can actually agree to a camera pilot.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is entirely my own decision, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers the choice, the two options are distinct and plain, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: Nothing I typed is changed here, and the generic line stays true to my wanting carriers to try it, though it does not say that a terminal's trial needs its manager and head office to agree.

screens.why1: Choosing who fronts the interview belongs here, just before the study goes out to dock supervisors, and it has not been asked before.
screens.why2: The question is clear and says dock supervisors, but the hint packs in video, typing, voice recording, credits and text links, so I need a second read to see what I am deciding.
screens.why3: I can listen to two 5-second clips and pick the voice I think a dock supervisor would stay on the line with.
screens.why4: Two voices with samples are distinct and enough, and the preselection covers not caring, but the names say nothing about how each one differs, so I have to play both to compare them.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor, dock supervisors, in the question and changes nothing I typed about the product.
screens.instead: Who should ask dock supervisors your questions? Pick a voice; it costs 400 credits either way, and people can also read and tap their answers. Options: Daphne (preselected), Saskia, each with a 5-second sample.

screens.why1: I just chose who asks the questions, so deciding how dock supervisors answer is the obvious last step before sending the study.
screens.why2: The choices are clear, but "Hear her Still recording · ready in a few minutes" runs together on first read, and the 9-in-10 line takes a second look.
screens.why3: I know my dock supervisors work on a loud floor between trailers and carry a phone or scanner, so I can pick from what I know of their shift.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, but the first option's recording status is mashed into its description and "Ready when Daphne is" is vague next to "Ready now".
screens.why5: It says dock supervisors, my own people, and changes nothing I typed about the study.
screens.instead: How should dock supervisors answer? Options: Daphne, an AI interviewer, asks aloud and they talk, type or tap (ready in a few minutes; catches more than 9 in 10 spoken answers on a loud dock) / They read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose when they open the link (ready in a few minutes).

screens.why1: Right after choosing how dock supervisors will answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who receives the link.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly on first pass, and the Contacts page mention is clear enough in context for a founder using the tool.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach, since we have talked to more than 50 trucking companies and work with several LTL carriers, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my case, but a by-name list and a Keel search list both end in individual links, so the line between them turns on where the names came from, and the open-link option's Google sign-in is a poor fit for dock staff who may not have or use a Google account at work.
screens.why5: My pick of people I know by name is kept as typed, and nothing on the screen changes what I said about dock supervisors.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" is plain and the cards back it, but the number beside it, "3 holding · 7 people answered", doesn't say 3 of 3 cards and at first reads like 3 of 7 people.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart on this page, but each card line gives the count and bar ("4 of 5 ... bar 4 of 5"); I need a second look to square the 5 with the 7 who answered, and the page never says why 2 are missing.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, including my "every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample", though the statement above them is clumsy.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for Transload or what to do next, such as whether to check camera coverage at the doors before a pilot, and the only explanatory line describes how the verdict is worked out.
screens.why_b5: It stays with the people who answered and marks "at the bar" and "1 on a condition" honestly, but a flat "Holding up" rests on 5 counted people, with two cards exactly at the bar, no low-n warning and no reason for the 2 left out.
screens.instead: All 3 beliefs held, but on only 5 of the 7 who answered (say why 2 weren't counted), and two sit exactly at the bar, so one answer would flip them: treat this as an early signal, and check camera coverage at the scan doors in your first terminals before you rely on it.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "4 of 5 said yes or yes, with some steps · bar 4 of 5 · at the bar", so I can see the belief held and that it only just cleared.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly shows 3 yes, 1 with some steps and 1 no over 5 counted people, with my bar marked at 4 of 5 and the strip agreeing.
screens.why_b3: The name Compatibility and the line about cameras covering the doors where freight is scanned are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me door coverage isn't the blocker for this group and sends me to adoption friction as the thing to look at next, which is a concrete next read for the idea.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible and the count line says "a lean, not a call", but the So line flatly says cameras are "not what will stop them" on 5 people sitting exactly at the bar, with one small terminal having no door cameras at all.
screens.instead: Among these 5, cameras mostly covered the doors, which is a lean and only just at the bar; the one no is a small terminal with nothing pointing at its doors, so check small terminals before selling there, and look at adoption friction next.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "4 of 5 said it would have gone better", with the bar at 4 of 5, so the verdict and its deciding number are tied together.
screens.why_b2: On first look I can see it counts better against same, over 5 counted people, with 4 a lot, 0 a little, 1 same, and the bar at 4 of 5.
screens.why_b3: The name and belief line are the ones I checked, including my words "every undercharged shipment caught, not just a sample".
screens.why_b4: The So line correctly points me to Adoption friction as the next question, but doesn't say what this result means for selling Transload or what to do about the one supervisor who saw no difference.
screens.why_b5: It keeps 6 answered and 5 counted visible, explains why Hamid is left out, calls this a small group and "a lean, not a call", flags it as hypothetical, and says only that they "imagined" it going better.
screens.instead: 4 of 5 imagined their last shipment going better, right at your bar, so one more 'no difference' would drop it: find out why Dwayne saw none and whether terminals like his are worth selling to, then check Adoption friction to see whether supervisors would review the flags.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside "5 of 5 would do it, bar 4 of 5, 1 on a condition", so I have both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The four answer rows with their counts, the 5 counted and the marker at 4 of 5 are all plain on first look, and the 1-in-3 wording works out to the same bar.
screens.why_b3: The Adoption friction name and "review each shipment the system flags" are the words I checked on the way in, and the question uses them too.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and promises that what would make it worth it is below, but Dwayne's list entry gives no condition, so I don't know what to change or do next for the flag review.
screens.why_b5: The 5 counted stay visible, Hamid's guess is excluded and named, the conditional yes is split out, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps the 5 of 5 from reading as proof.
screens.instead: 4 of 5 would review each flag as is, and Dwayne would only if [his condition, in his words]; on 5 people that's a lean, so keep flag review in the design and test Dwayne's condition with the next dock supervisors.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and the deciding number sit together in "Holding up, 4 of 5 said yes or yes, with some steps, bar 4 of 5, at the bar", repeated in "Compatibility held, 4 of 5".
screens.why_b3: The dimension name and the belief about cameras covering the doors where freight is scanned are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The screen implies I should look at terminals like Teresa's with no door coverage, but it never says what the result means for the idea, such as qualifying terminals on door coverage before selling or whether the line is safe at the bar.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible and the count is honest, but "held" at exactly the bar on 5 people is never called thin, one more no would flip it, and the "2 asked their why here" count leaves unclear why only one of the four yes answers appears.
screens.why_b6: Teresa's yard-and-gate cameras add a real detail I had not typed, that small terminals may have cameras pointed at the wrong places, but Dwayne's answer under the steps question is about late trailers and short crews and tells me nothing about what steps camera coverage took.
screens.instead: Compatibility held at the bar, 4 of 5, and one more no would drop it: small terminals may have cameras only on the yard and gate, so ask about door coverage before you sell, and note that the one answer on steps did not say what the steps were.

screens.why1: As an opening screen, it makes sense to first ask whether freight outran measuring on my dock this week, before asking for the story.
screens.why2: I get it on first read, but freight doesn't "cross faster than it could be measured" in my words; I'd say it went through without getting dimensioned because there wasn't time.
screens.why3: I run the shift and decide what gets measured, so I know from the last five working days without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but "I can't recall one particular shipment" doesn't fit a question about the whole dock over a week, and a second chip, "I'd rather not say," is one more than this needs.
screens.why5: It keeps the idea of freight outrunning measurement, and nothing about a product or company reaches me.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question ending in "Yes or no," which I can hear once and answer right away.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did any freight leave your dock unmeasured because there wasn't time? Yes or No.

screens.why1: After asking whether freight outran our measuring this week, it makes sense to show me an idea for measuring it and the card is labelled as that.
screens.why2: Barcode scan, freight and paperwork are my daily words, but the opening line 'flagged shipments with video evidence' doesn't tell me what the thing is until the next sentences, and 'fits a 3D box' takes me a second, since on my dock we'd say it gets the dimensions.
screens.why3: I run a terminal with security cameras, scanners and freight that gets billed on its paperwork, so I can picture exactly how this would land on my shift.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options, chips or box.
screens.why5: It's shown on purpose as an idea and the belief is marked as the builders', but the first line is a feature-pitch fragment rather than saying what Transload is, such as software that measures freight from cameras.
screens.why6: The short sentences say fine and I can hold them, but the opening 'Transload, flagged shipments with video evidence' is a clumsy fragment to hear, 'it' changes footing across 'fits a 3D box to it', and 'video evidence' comes twice in a short read.
screens.instead: Imagine Transload, software that measures freight from your security cameras. It measures every shipment in the background, matches each barcode scan to the freight on video, and flags shipments bigger than their paperwork, with the video as evidence. The people building it believe this would mean no change to how your dock works.

screens.why1: Right after a card about flagged shipments with video evidence, it makes sense to ask whether my doors already have cameras on them.
screens.why2: Cameras, doors and scanning are all my words, but "your last shipment" reads like I shipped something, when I run a shift moving hundreds of them, and I don't scan freight myself, my dock crew does.
screens.why3: I know which of my doors have cameras, but no single shipment stands out as my last one and I'd be answering for the terminal rather than for a freight scan I did myself.
screens.why4: Yes and No fit and the escape works, but "Yes, with some steps" is odd because a camera either covers a door or it doesn't, and the answer I'd actually give, only some doors, is missing.
screens.why5: The video evidence idea is kept and nothing leaks beyond the card, but the card's clipped "flagged shipments with video evidence" doesn't say who flags what, and "where you scanned" drifts away from my job of running the shift.
screens.why6: It is short and says well as one question with three options, but "yes, with some steps" makes no sense when heard against a question about cameras, so I'd have to stop and work out what it means.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. Did cameras already cover the dock doors where your crew scanned freight? All of them; most of them; a few of them; or none. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the camera question, it makes sense to ask whether this would have helped on the freight I just had in mind.
screens.why2: The words are simple, but a supervisor doesn't think in one 'shipment' or say it 'went better'; I'd want to know better how: billing, speed or fewer disputes.
screens.why3: Hundreds of shipments cross my dock on a shift, so 'my last shipment' is a bit arbitrary, and from one line on the card I'd partly guess what flagged video would have changed on it.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' is the honest way out when I don't know enough about the product.
screens.why5: The name and idea are shown on purpose so nothing leaks, but 'flagged shipments with video evidence' says little, and a vague 'go better' drifts from getting freight billed at true size without slowing the dock.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, with four short options I can hold after one hearing and a single escape at the end, though 'or not' followed by a list is slightly redundant.
screens.instead: Think of the last shipment you had re-measured: would Transload have helped you bill it at its true size without slowing the dock? A lot; A little; No difference; It would have made things worse; or I can't tell.

screens.why1: After being shown the idea and asked if it would have helped, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually do the work it needs from me.
screens.why2: I get the question on first hearing, but "flags" leaves me unsure what a flag means here, whether it's a short-measured shipment, a density mismatch or something else.
screens.why3: I know what my shift can absorb, but I'd be guessing because it doesn't say how many flags a shift would throw or how long each review takes, and on a busy dock that decides it.
screens.why4: The range is complete and the escape fits, but "Yes, if it was clearly worth it" and "Probably not" both hedge and overlap, since my probably not is really a no unless it pays.
screens.why5: It's a plain ask about the review step on the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of anyone's plans or internal terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and the four options are easy to hold after hearing them once, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: To use Transload, you'd review each shipment it flags on your shift, on top of your other work. Would you do that, or not? Yes; yes, if it was clearly worth it; probably not; or no. Or say you can't tell.
